{{Short description|American-British chemist (born 1946)}}
'''Russell P. Hughes''' (born December 23, 1946)  an American/British chemist, is the Frank R. Mori Professor Emeritus and research professor in the  Department of Chemistry at [[Dartmouth College]]. His research interests are in [[organometallic chemistry]], with emphasis on the chemistry of [[transition metal]] complexes interacting with fluorocarbons. His research group's work in this area led to several creative syntheses of complexes of transition metal and perfluorinated hydrocarbon fragments.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Hughes|first=Russell P.|date=2010-11-01|title=Fluorine as a ligand substituent in organometallic chemistry: A second chance and a second research career|journal=Journal of Fluorine Chemistry|series=2010 ACS Award Issue "For Creative Work in Fluorine Chemistry" Russell P. Hughes|volume=131|issue=11|pages=1059–1070|doi=10.1016/j.jfluchem.2010.06.014}}</ref>

== Education ==
Hughes was born on December 23, 1946, in [[Denbigh]], Wales, the son of Elliot and Joan (Profit) Hughes. He earned his B.Sc. at the [[University of Manchester]] Institute of Science and Technology, and his Ph.D. at the [[University of Toronto]] under John Powell.  He held postdoctoral fellowships at the [[University of Bristol]] in Michael Green's laboratory and at [[McGill University]] with John Harrod.<ref name="d">[http://chemistry.dartmouth.edu/news-events/fluorine-chemistry-symposium/russell-p-hughes] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220191127/http://chemistry.dartmouth.edu/news-events/fluorine-chemistry-symposium/russell-p-hughes |date=2016-12-20 }} Faculty page at Dartmouth></ref>

== Research career ==
Hughes began his independent scientific career as an assistant professor at [[Dartmouth College]] in 1976.  He was promoted to associate professor in 1982, and Professor in 1986.  He chaired the department of Chemistry from 1991 to 1994. In 1999, he was appointed to be the Inaugural Frank R. Mori Professor in the Arts & Sciences.  His research has centered on organometallic chemistry, with focus on the chemistry of transition metal complexes interacting with fluorocarbons and the organometallic chemistry of small organic rings.<ref name=":0" />  After 35 years of experimental work, he transitioned to [[computational chemistry]] and collaborative research.<ref name=d />

== Honors ==
Hughes is a Fellow of the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]], the [[American Chemical Society]], the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], the  [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]], and the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]. The American Chemical Society awarded him the Award for Creative Work in Fluorine Chemistry in 2010.<ref name=d />

== Research highlights ==

=== Metal complexes of octafluorocyclooctatetraene (OFCOT) ===
One of Hughes’ research interests focused on the study of transition metal complexes with octafluoro[[cyclooctatetraene]] (OFCOT), and the comparison of the structural features of these complexes to the hydrocarbon counterpart of OFCOT cyclooctatetraene (COT).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Barefoot|first1=Aldos C.|last2=Corcoran|first2=Edward W.|last3=Hughes|first3=Russell P.|last4=Lemal|first4=David M.|last5=Saunders|first5=W. Daniel|last6=Laird|first6=Brian B.|last7=Davis|first7=Raymond E.|date=1981-02-01|title=Octafluorocyclooctatetraene transition-metal chemistry: 1,2-.eta. and 1,2,3,6-.eta. complexes of iron and platinum|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=103|issue=4|pages=970–972|doi=10.1021/ja00394a057|issn=0002-7863}}</ref>  One striking difference in the coordination complexes of OFCOT is that their thermal stability and resistance to dynamic rearrangements in binding geometry (diminished fluxional character) compared to COT analogs.<ref name=":0" />  These differences can be rationalized based on the relative thermodynamic stability of the isomers computed using [[density functional theory]] (DFT).<ref name=":0" />
[[File:Octafluorocyclooctatetraene.png|center|frameless|288x288px|Differences in interactions of transition metals with cyclooctatetraene (COT) vs octafluorocyclooctatetraene (OFCOT)]]

===Complexes of perfluorocyclopentadienyl ligand ===
In 1992, Hughes and coworkers used flash vacuum [[pyrolysis]] (at 770&nbsp;°C) to extrude CO from an oxacyclohexadienyl complex afford the first [[metallocene]] containing a perfluorinated cyclopentadienyl ring, η<sup>5</sup>-C<sub>5</sub>F<sub>5</sub>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Curnow|first1=Owen J.|last2=Hughes|first2=Russell P.|date=1992-07-01|title=[Ru(.eta.5-C5Me5)(.eta.5-C5F5)]: the first transition-metal complex containing a perfluorocyclopentadienyl ligand|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=114|issue=14|pages=5895–5897|doi=10.1021/ja00040a083|issn=0002-7863}}</ref> [[Ruthenocene]] and its perfluorocyclopentadienyl analog were compared.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Hughes|first1=Russell P.|last2=Zheng|first2=Xiaoming|last3=Ostrander|first3=Robert L.|last4=Rheingold|first4=Arnold L.|date=1994-05-01|title=Synthesis and Molecular Structure of [Ru(.eta.5-C5H5)(.eta.5-C5F5)]. Intramolecular Structural Comparison of the Cyclopentadienyl Ligand with its Perfluorinated Analog|journal=Organometallics|volume=13|issue=5|pages=1567–1568|doi=10.1021/om00017a011|issn=0276-7333}}</ref> It was observed that the C<sub>5</sub>F<sub>5</sub> interaction with Ru results in a shorter distance between this ring and Ru, compared to the hydrocarbon analog.<ref name=":1" />
[[File:Ruthenocene and its perfluorocyclopentadienyl analog.png|center|frameless|240x240px|Structural differences in ruthenocene to its perfluorocyclopentadienyl analog]]

=== Perfluorobenzyne complexes===
Hughes and coworkers synthesized to the first transition metal complex of perfluorobenzyne (C<sub>6</sub>F<sub>4</sub>).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hughes|first1=Russell P.|last2=Williamson|first2=Alex|last3=Sommer|first3=Roger D.|last4=Rheingold|first4=Arnold L.|date=2001-08-01|title=The First Transition Metal Complex of Tetrafluorobenzyne: Ir(η5-C5Me5)(PMe3)(η2-C6F4)|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=123|issue=30|pages=7443–7444|doi=10.1021/ja010992o|pmid=11472184|issn=0002-7863}}</ref>
[[File:Perfluorobenzyne.png|center|frameless|152x152px|perfluorobenzyne]]

=== Perfluorocarbene Complexes ===
In 2005, through an inner-sphere reduction reaction of perfluoroalkyl ligands Hughes and coworkers provided a novel and useful route to difluorocarbene and perfluoroalkylidene complexes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hughes|first1=Russell P.|last2=Laritchev|first2=Roman B.|last3=Yuan|first3=Jian|last4=Golen|first4=James A.|last5=Rucker|first5=Adam N.|last6=Rheingold|first6=Arnold L.|date=2005-11-01|title=A Simple Route to Difluorocarbene and Perfluoroalkylidene Complexes of Iridium|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=127|issue=43|pages=15020–15021|doi=10.1021/ja055166k|pmid=16248629|issn=0002-7863}}</ref>  This was followed in 2007 by the synthesis of the first, and so far, the only, example of a carbene ligand bearing two strongly electron withdrawing perfluoroalkyl groups.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yuan|first1=Jian|last2=Hughes|first2=Russell P.|last3=Rheingold|first3=Arnold L.|date=2007-10-01|title=The First Example of a Bis(trifluoromethyl)carbene Transition-Metal Complex and Its Reduction to a Perfluoroallene Complex|journal=European Journal of Inorganic Chemistry|language=en|volume=2007|issue=30|pages=4723–4725|doi=10.1002/ejic.200700814|issn=1099-0682}}</ref>
[[File:Perfluorocarbene Complex.png|center|frameless|130x130px|
perfluorocarbene complex]]

=== Complex of fluoromethyne==
In 2006, Hughes and coworkers prepared a complex of CF by reduction of a Mo-trifluoromethyl complex.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Huang|first1=Hui|last2=Hughes|first2=Russell P.|last3=Landis|first3=Clark R.|last4=Rheingold|first4=Arnold L.|date=2006-06-01|title=The Simplest Binary Fluorocarbon as a Ligand. Synthetic, Spectroscopic, Crystallographic, and Computational Studies of a Molybdenum Complex of Terminally Ligated Carbon Monofluoride (Fluoromethylidyne)|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=128|issue=23|pages=7454–7455|doi=10.1021/ja062510k|pmid=16756295|issn=0002-7863}}</ref>
